title: Angel
description: Supernatural being in religions and mythologies
wiki_lead:
An angel is a spiritual, heavenly, or supernatural entity, often depicted as humanoid with bird-like wings, frequently in the role as a messenger or intermediary between God (the transcendent) and humanity (the profane) in various traditions like the Abrahamic religions. Other roles include protectors and guides for humans, such as guardian angels, and servants of God. In Western belief-systems the term is often used to distinguish benevolent from malevolent intermediary beings. 
Emphasizing the distance between God and mankind, revelation-based belief-systems require angels to bridge the gap between the earthly and the transcendent realm. Angels play a lesser role in monistic belief-systems, since the gap is non-existent. However, angelic beings might be conceived as aids to achieve a proper relationship with the divine.
Abrahamic religions describe angelic hierarchies, which vary by religion and sect. Some angels are indicated with names (such as Gabriel or Michael) or are of a specific kind or rank (such as a seraph or an archangel). Malevolent angels are often believed to have been expelled from heaven and are called fallen angels. In many such religions, the devil (or devils) is identified with such angels.

Angels in art are often identified with bird wings, halos, and divine light. They are usually shaped like humans of extraordinary beauty, though this is not always the case – sometimes, they are portrayed as being frightening or inhuman.

Etymology, names

The word angel arrives in modern English from Old English engel (with a hard g) and the Old French angele. Both of these derive from Late Latin angelus, which in turn was borrowed from Late Greek ἄγγελος angelos (literally "messenger"). Τhe word's earliest form is Mycenaean a-ke-ro, attested in Linear B syllabic script. According to the Dutch linguist R. S. P. Beekes, ángelos itself may be "an Oriental loan, like ἄγγαρος (ángaros, 'Persian mounted courier')."
The rendering of ángelos is the Septuagint's default translation of the Biblical Hebrew term malʼākh, denoting simply "messenger" without connoting its nature. In the Latin Vulgate, this meaning becomes bifurcated: when malʼākh or ángelos is supposed to denote a human messenger, words like nuntius or legatus are applied. If the word refers to some supernatural being, the word angelus appears. Such differentiation has been taken over by later vernacular translations of the Bible, early Christian and Jewish exegetes and eventually modern scholars.


Background
The concept of angels is historically best to be understood from different ideas of the concept of God throughout history. In polytheistic and animistic worldviews, supernatural powers (i.e. deities, spirits, daemons, etc.) were assigned to different natural phenomena. Within a monotheistic framework, these powers were reconsidered to be servants of the supreme deity, turning autonomous supernatural beings into "angels".
By that, supernatural powers controlling or influencing humanity's perception of the world, including natural phenomena and humans, are ultimately under control of a supreme God. Prominent angels, such as Michael and Gabriel, reflect a connection to the Chief Semitic deity El. Even "bad" angels such as Satan, Samael, Iblis etc., can be understood as an operating force within the nature of humans, as responsible for selfish tendencies.
The idea of angels in early Hebrew scripture as supernatural agents is absent. Instead, the Hebrew deity intervenes in human affairs, mostly by means of punishment. Only in later thought of post-exilic and prophetic writings, the Biblical deity is conceptualized as distant and more merciful, his interventions replaced by the idea of angels. However, such angels still carry out the gruesome attributes of God and can be both benevolent and malevolent. grok_lead: An angel is a supernatural, non-divine spiritual being in the Abrahamic religions â Judaism, Christianity, and Islam âprimarily serving as a messenger between God and humanity, relaying divine information, accompanying the divine presence, and carrying out God's will, such as assisting or intervening in human affairs. The term "angel" derives from the Hebrew mal'akh (plural mal'akhim), meaning "messenger," and its equivalents in Greek ( angelos) and Arabic ( malak), emphasizing their role as intermediaries rather than objects of worship. In Jewish tradition, angels appear in the Hebrew Bible as anthropomorphic figures who often manifest in human form, such as the three visitors to Abraham in Genesis 18, and perform tasks like delivering prophecies or protecting the faithful, though they are typically unnamed in pre-exilic texts, with named figures like Gabriel and Michael first appearing in the Book of Daniel. Christian theology builds on this foundation, viewing angels as purely spiritual entities with intellect and free will. In some Christian traditions, such as Catholicism, they are organized in a hierarchy of nine choirs, where they announce key events in salvation history, such as Gabriel 's annunciation to Mary in Luke 1, and engage in spiritual warfare under leaders like Michael. In Islam, angels are created from light as obedient, luminous beings without free will, tasked with recording human deeds, delivering revelationsâlike Gabriel (Jibril) to Muhammad âand maintaining cosmic order, underscoring their role in total submission to Allah. Angels in Abrahamic religions are generally described as intelligent spiritual beings; in Christianity, they possess moral agency through free will, allowing for the possibility of rebellion as depicted in some interpretations; in Judaism and Islam, they are typically seen as obedient without the capacity to sin or exercise independent moral choice, though some Judeo-Christian apocryphal texts (such as the Book of Enoch) describe rebellious fallen angels. Notable angelic classes include archangels, such as Michael ("Who is like God?"), the protector and warrior prince of the heavenly host mentioned in Daniel, Jude, and Revelation; Gabriel ("God is my strength"), the interpreter of visions and divine announcer in all three faiths; and Raphael ("God heals"), the guide and healer from the deuterocanonical Book of Tobit (accepted in Catholic and Orthodox canons). Other types, like cherubim and seraphim, serve as throne guardians or worshippers in visions from Isaiah and Ezekiel, highlighting angels' diverse functions beyond mere messaging to include praise, protection, and judgment. Across these traditions, angels are created beings, finite and subordinate to God, distinct from humans yet capable of interacting with the material world when divinely directed. No major Abrahamic religious texts describe angels as created from the "breath of life," "God's breath," or "energy." In the Bible, the "breath of life" (Genesis 2:7) animates humans specifically, making Adam a living being, while angels are portrayed as spiritual beings without any specified material substance. In Islam, angels are created from light (nur) according to Hadith traditions.
